title: Gilpin County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Gilpin County well depths center around 250 ft, with most between 150-380 ft. Learn about yields, costs, and water levels for wells in Gilpin County.
h1: Water wells in Gilpin County, Colorado
intro_html:
Gilpin County wells are classic mountain bedrock wells: most are in fractured granite or gneiss, not in a big sand aquifer. The state has records on 4,554 well permits here, with depth, yield, and water-level data on a good share of them. That gives you a realistic picture of how deep you’re likely to drill, how much water most people get, and what that means for cost and risk on a rural property.

Here’s how the numbers shake out for Gilpin County as a whole, including the areas around Black Hawk, Central, and Rollinsville.

sections.heading: How deep Gilpin County wells usually are
sections.html:
Across Gilpin County, reported total depths cluster around a median of 250 feet, with the middle half of wells between 150 and 380 feet. About 13% are under 100 feet, 45% fall between 100 and 300, 35% run 300 to 600, and 7% go past 600 feet. The deepest well on record makes it all the way to 1,401 feet.

For budgeting, most new holes in this fractured-bedrock terrain end up in that 150–380 foot band, but you need to be prepared for the occasional deep one toward 500 feet or more, especially on higher ridges. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells here, so you’re relying entirely on local fractured rock, which is why depths vary so much even between neighboring properties.

sections.heading: How much water Gilpin wells produce
sections.html:
On the 1,415 wells that report a tested yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.0 and 10.0 gpm. That’s solid for a mountain county and easily covers a typical exempt household-use well plus some outdoor watering inside the rules.

Low producers exist but are a small slice: about 2% of reported wells come in under 1 gpm, and 27% are in the 1–5 gpm range. The bulk, 63%, fall between 5 and 15 gpm, and 7% exceed 15 gpm. In fractured granite and crystalline rock like this, yields are controlled by how many good fractures your driller hits, not by a uniform water table, so there’s always some unpredictability from lot to lot.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they suggest
sections.html:
For the 307 wells with static water-level data, the median depth to water is about 50 feet below ground, with the middle half between 30 and 82 feet. So even though total well depths often run a couple hundred feet, water commonly stands within the first hundred feet of the hole.

By decade, median measured water levels were around 35 feet in the 1960s and 1970s, 32 feet in the 1990s, then deeper at 70 feet in the 2010s, and 50 feet in the 2020s. That hints at somewhat deeper water levels in more recent readings, but the data set is small. In bedrock systems like Gilpin County, short-term drops can reflect local pumping and dry cycles more than a county-wide decline.

sections.heading: Who drilled here and when
sections.html:
Gilpin County’s drilling history is spread out but peaked in the 1970s and 1990s. The state shows 979 permits issued in the 1970s, 500 in the 1980s, 957 in the 1990s, 649 in the 2000s, 349 in the 2010s, and 225 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. Earlier activity goes back to at least the 1950s, with 37 permits that decade and 198 in the 1960s.

The work has been concentrated among a few drillers. C. R. Smith Drilling (Calvin R. Smith) appears on 885 wells, C R Smith Drilling Inc (Frank Smith) on 645, and Ground Water Systems Inc (Richard R. Wilson) on 415. If you’re looking at an older home near Black Hawk, Central, Rollinsville, or over the line toward Clear Creek or Boulder counties, there’s a good chance one of those names is on the log.

sections.heading: Expected drilling and complete-well costs
sections.html:
Gilpin County sits on fractured mountain bedrock, mainly granite and gneiss, so drilling is slow and hard on tools. Typical local pricing runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 250-foot median depth, just the drilled hole pencils out to roughly $16,200–$25,000.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that median depth usually ends up around $22,200–$37,000. If you’re on a higher ridge or in an area where nearby wells run closer to the 380-foot mark, adjust your budget upward accordingly. In Gilpin’s fractured-rock setting, having your driller pull logs for nearby wells in both Gilpin and adjacent Jefferson or Boulder counties is worth the time before you close on a lot.

sections.heading: Risks: low yield, mines, and contamination
sections.html:
Gilpin’s bedrock geology means yield risk is real: a small share of wells, about 2% of those with tests, come in under 1 gpm. Those can still work with storage, but they’re less forgiving if your household demand is high. Depth is also variable, with 7% of wells deeper than 600 feet, which can push costs up fast.

On the environmental side, state and federal maps show 4,519 historic mine features, 42 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, and 30 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t mean your well is contaminated, but it does mean you should test for metals and, in some areas, PFAS, especially around older mining districts between Central and Black Hawk or toward Clear Creek County.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Gilpin County
sections.html:
If you’re looking at vacant land, DWR records show 3,267 wells recorded as constructed out of 4,554 permits, and 3,309 report a total depth. Use those nearby well logs to triangulate a realistic depth and yield expectation for your specific parcel.

Most permits here, about 92%, are domestic or household use, with small shares for stock and monitoring, and virtually none for irrigation. Plan your landscaping and any outbuildings around that. When you design a new home, leave space and access for a well rig and for a septic system that meets current code in shallow, rocky soils. Check local data from neighboring Boulder, Jefferson, and Clear Creek counties if you are near a county line; geology doesn’t stop at the border, and neither do drilling conditions.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Gilpin County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on 3,309 wells that report total depth, the median well in Gilpin County is about 250 feet deep. The middle half of wells run between 150 and 380 feet. About 13% are shallower than 100 feet, 45% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 35% are 300 to 600 feet, and 7% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest recorded at 1,401 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Gilpin County?
faq.a: For the 1,415 wells with pump-test data, the median yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half fall between 4.0 and 10.0 gpm. Low producers under 1 gpm make up about 2% of reported wells. Most wells provide 5–15 gpm, which covers a normal household-use well under Colorado’s exempt rules, with some margin if you manage outdoor use sensibly.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Gilpin County?
faq.a: In Gilpin County’s fractured granite and gneiss, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 250-foot median depth, that’s roughly $16,200–$25,000 for the hole alone. A complete well with casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $22,200–$37,000 at that depth. Deeper wells toward 400–500 feet will scale that cost up accordingly.

faq.q: Is Gilpin County well water safe to drink?
faq.a: Many homes in Gilpin County rely on private wells, but safety depends on location and testing, not just depth. There are 4,519 historic mine features, 42 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, and 30 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped within about 10 miles. Because of that mining and PFAS history, it’s smart to test a well for metals and, where appropriate, PFAS, and to retest regularly, especially near older mining districts.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Gilpin County wells?
faq.a: Static water-level data from 307 wells show medians around 35 feet below ground in the 1960s and 1970s, 32 feet in the 1990s, then deeper at 70 feet in the 2010s and 50 feet in the 2020s. That suggests somewhat deeper levels in more recent measurements, but the sample is limited. In fractured bedrock, local conditions and short-term climate can affect levels as much as long-term regional trends.
